newsitem.title: INDIA: U.S. wants lower phone rates with India.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wants lower phone rates with India.

text.p: The United States has told Indian and American telephone companies that they must set dramatically lower phone call rates by 2002 to curb over-pricing and help contain a growing U.S. balance of payments problem.

U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) chairman Reed Hundt said his agency has told American telephone companies that the basic cost of a call from the United States to India must be cut to no more than 23 cents a minute, down from 80 cents now.
"We are shaking the pillars of these very high prices, saying we will not approve very high settlement rates," Hundt told a group of reporters in New Delhi during a visit to India.
U.S. companies and India's state-run international telephone monopoly, Videsh Sanchar Nigam Ltd (VSNL), are renegotiating the rates that people pay to make calls between the two countries.
Currently it costs far less to place a call from the United States to India than in the other direction.
The base "settlement rate" for a call from the United States to India currently is about 80 cents a minute, Hundt said. In the other direction, the rate is about $2.30.
But the final cost to the caller is more than the base rate because the telephone companies add on a margin.
The FCC has influence in the matter because it must approve any deal between VSNL and U.S. firms before it can take effect.

"We are looking for an agreement that at the end of some period will have a settlement rate of not more than 23 cents a minute," Hundt said, adding that the rate would apply to calls from the United States to India.
He did not say what rate the FCC would like for calls from India to the United States, although he said it should be lower.
"That's the objective that has to be negotiated for," Hundt said, adding that the new rate would have to come into effect by January 1, 2002.
The U.S. regulator said international rates had historically been much higher than the cost to the telephone companies, which often use the revenue to subsidise domestic rates.
Increased competition, especially in the United States, has reduced rates, but Hundt said they remained high. He said the average cost of a call from the United States was $1 a minute.
"That's crazy," he said. "It should be more like 10 cents a minute."
Under a pact at the World Trade Organisation, signatories including India will have to open up their telephone sectors to competition by 2004, meaning VSNL's monopoly will end by then.

In the meantime, it costs much less to call from the United States to most other countries than in the other direction, spurring demand for call-back services. These allow someone telephoning the United States to be immediately called back at the much lower rate.

Because bilateral agreements require U.S. telephone companies to share some of the revenue with their foreign counterparts, large amounts of dollars are flowing out of the United States, creating a balance of payments problem, Hundt said.

"The world's phone calls all appear to emanate from the United States," he said, noting that U.S. consumers are paying $6 billion in additional telephone costs every year to cover the amount of money that American companies are sending overseas.

"This dwarfs our foreign aid budget," he said. "For a year we've said this has to stop. If it continues, all international telephony will be paid by the U.S. It is tremendously unacceptable and a drain on the balance of payments."
